Canonical transport with consistent weights ​

The canonical transport takes a given canonical map of , the same for all markers, and then chooses the weights so that the markers represent the same density . The analysis uses the continuum limit, in which the markers form a density in phase space.

Transport ​

The continuum description is that of Liouville's theorem for the marker density: the markers have a smooth density   and a smooth weight field  , they represent   , and the sheet map     carries them to the canonical marker density

under the single-sheet condition   of the velocity–momentum fold. This chapter treats one layer of a folded sheet. The canonical map transports the canonical density to   .

The identity of the proof holds to a relative error of   (Simpson's rule) for a canonical density and a weight field that depends on , and the frozen-weight density fails it by   (test/remapping/transport.jl):

julia
using ParticleRemapping
m = 1.3
ñ(X, P) = (1 + 0.3sin(X)) * exp(-P^2 / 2) * (1 + 0.2P^2)
W(X, V) = 1 + 0.3cos(X) + 0.2tanh(V)
dWV(X, V) = W(X, V) + 0.2V * sech(V)^2                  # ∂_V (W V)
pts = [(X, V) for X in (0.4, 2.1) for V in (-2.5, -0.7, 0.9, 3.0)]
exact = represented_density(ñ, W, dWV; m)
frozen = represented_density(ñ, W, dWV; m, frozen = true)
(exact = maximum(cumulative_current_error(exact, ñ, W, X, V; m) for (X, V) in pts),
    frozen = minimum(cumulative_current_error(frozen, ñ, W, X, V; m) for (X, V) in pts))
(exact = 1.8277027920094342e-14, frozen = 0.05053416034698918)

The limit ​

For a Maxwellian,   for  , so a uniform marker distribution with consistent weights does not even form a single sheet. In general the equimeasurability fails as well. A smooth canonical map with consistent weights can therefore rearrange the canonical marker density, but it cannot make the marker distribution uniform. In particular it cannot fill a region in which is small: it can only move that region, for example into the tails of , where few markers are needed. This is the obstruction holes persist of one map for all markers, stated for consistent weights.

Admissible canonical maps ​

Example (cotangent lift)

Let   , whose flow is  ,   with  . Here   and  , so the bracket becomes    , using    . Up to the factor this is   . The lift is admissible if and only if and are constant, that is   , which requires to be constant, as for an that is even in . The flow then keeps the profile exactly,    (the closed-form example derives this). This map moves markers in , faster where the current is small. It is not designed to equidistribute.

The cotangent lift is cotangent_lift, its flow cotangent_lift_flow (the classical Runge–Kutta method on ). Cotangent lifts are among the elementary canonical maps; the sliced redistribution composes sliced quantile cotangent lifts.

The set of admissible generators is a linear space. A practical remap can choose from a finite basis, impose the linear constraints of the proposition for both branches, and pick the coefficients that decrease a measure of marker clustering.
